4069.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown II
4069.explanationMarkdown:
### Dynamic programming over completed trading days

The holding fee depends on the entire duration of a transaction, so the profit of a sale cannot be determined from its selling price alone. Try every earlier buying day for each possible selling day.

Let `dp[t]` be the largest profit from transactions completed within the first `t` days, with no stock left in hand. Initially every entry is zero: choosing no transactions is always allowed.

For a sale on day `j`, first keep `dp[j]`, the best result without selling that day. For every buying day `i < j`, consider the profit of buying on `i` and selling on `j`:

`prices[j] - prices[i] - costs[j - i]`.

A preceding sale must occur no later than day `i - cooldown - 1`. That means its profit is already summarized by `dp[max(i - cooldown, 0)]`. The transition is therefore:

`dp[j + 1] = max(dp[j], max_i(dp[max(i - cooldown, 0)] + prices[j] - prices[i] - costs[j - i]))`.

The code's expression `(i + 1) - (cooldown + 1)` is the same index `i - cooldown`. Notice that the fee is charged once per complete transaction; it is not a daily fee to multiply by the duration.

### Why the transition is complete

An optimal schedule through day `j` either makes no sale on that day or has a final transaction with some buying day `i`. In the latter case, everything before that purchase is an optimal compatible schedule within the prefix ending before the required cooldown. Replacing that prefix with `dp[max(i - cooldown, 0)]` cannot reduce the profit. Conversely, every transition joins a compatible prefix and one valid transaction, so it never violates the cooldown or holds two shares.

### Edge cases

A single day returns zero. Falling prices or fees that erase every gain also return zero. With `cooldown = 0`, a previous transaction may sell on day `i - 1`, but not on the new buying day. Buying and selling on the same day cannot help because fees are nonnegative, so considering only `i < j` is sufficient.
4069.timeComplexity: O(n²), where n is the number of trading days: each selling day examines all earlier buying days.
4069.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the prefix-profit DP array.
checks: Compared the supplied algorithm’s Python equivalent against an independent recursive enumeration of complete transaction schedules on 5,910 cases: lengths 1–4, prices in {1,2,3}, fees in {0,1}, and every permitted cooldown. All matched.
The checks include no possible transaction, zero cooldown, maximal cooldown, unprofitable fees, and multiple compatible transactions.

4072.title: Maximum Alternating Subarray Sum With One Deletion
4072.explanationMarkdown:
### Track retained-length parity and whether deletion has been used

Every chosen subarray starts with a plus sign. Appending a retained element alternates the sign; deleting an element does not change the parity of the retained length. These are exactly the two properties needed for a constant-size dynamic program.

Use four states `dp[used][parity]`. `used` is zero or one according to whether the deletion has been used. In the implementation, parity zero means an odd number of retained elements, so the last retained element was added; parity one means an even number, so the last retained element was subtracted. Each state represents a nonempty candidate reaching the current processed position, which may itself have been deleted.

For the next value `x`, calculate every transition from the previous states:

- Without deletion, an odd-length candidate is either a new singleton `[x]` or an even-length candidate extended by `+x`: `new[0][0] = max(old[0][1], 0) + x`.
- An even-length candidate without deletion must extend an odd-length candidate: `new[0][1] = old[0][0] - x`.
- With deletion used, an odd-length candidate either extends a previously deleted even-length candidate by `+x`, or deletes `x` from a no-deletion odd-length candidate: `new[1][0] = max(old[1][1] + x, old[0][0])`.
- Similarly, `new[1][1] = max(old[1][0] - x, old[0][1])`.

The code updates the deletion row first so its transitions still read the old no-deletion row. Each row assignment evaluates its entire right-hand side before replacing that row. Initialize all states and the answer to negative infinity, and take the best state after every position.

### Why this finds the optimum

At a position inside the candidate, the only legal choices are keeping that element or using the single deletion on it. Keeping toggles retained-length parity; deleting preserves it. The four transitions enumerate both choices and every possible starting position. Taking the maximum across positions allows the chosen subarray to end anywhere. Deleting an element outside the chosen subarray adds no useful option, since the same subarray is already considered with no deletion.

### Edge cases

The answer must be nonempty, even when every value is negative. In particular, a singleton negative input returns that negative value, not zero. A deletion can change the signs of every following retained element, so treating it as merely subtracting the removed value is incorrect. Use 64-bit integers in C++ because the answer can exceed a 32-bit signed integer; guard negative-infinity states before arithmetic.
4072.timeComplexity: O(n), where n is nums.length; each element updates four states.
checks: Compared the supplied algorithm’s Python equivalent against independently trying every optional deletion and every nonempty subarray of the resulting array. All 1,092 arrays of lengths 1–6 over {-2,0,3} matched.
The exhaustive checks include all-negative arrays, singleton inputs, deleting an interior element, and choosing not to delete.

4073.title: Count Good Strings
4073.explanationMarkdown:
### Reduce the recursive definition to odd-length runs

A maximal run is a consecutive block of one repeated character. A string is good exactly when all of its maximal runs have odd lengths.

For the forward direction, the base strings have one odd-length run. Joining two good strings at different boundary characters does not merge their end runs, so all runs remain odd. For the reverse direction, if every run is odd, each run is a base good string; concatenating the runs in order always joins different boundary characters and therefore constructs a good string.

Now choose the sequence of run lengths. They are positive odd integers summing to `n`. Once those lengths and the first character are fixed, the whole string is determined, because consecutive runs must alternate between `a` and `b`.

### Count the run-length sequences

Let `f[n]` count ordered compositions of `n` into positive odd parts. There is one such composition for `n = 1` and one for `n = 2`, so `f[1] = f[2] = 1`.

For `n >= 3`, split the compositions by their last part. If the last part is one, removing it leaves a composition of `n - 1`. Otherwise the last part is at least three; subtracting two from that last part gives a composition of `n - 2`. Both transformations are reversible, and the two cases are disjoint. Thus `f[n] = f[n - 1] + f[n - 2]`, the Fibonacci recurrence. Each composition allows two starting characters, so the answer is `2 * F[n]` with `F[0] = 0` and `F[1] = 1`.

### Compute the recurrence for a very large n

The transition matrix `T = [[1,1],[1,0]]` advances a pair of adjacent Fibonacci values. The code computes `T^n` by repeated squaring, multiplies it by the row vector `[2,0]`, and returns the second component. This is `2 * F[n]`.

Binary exponentiation processes the bits of `n`: multiply the accumulator by the current power when the bit is set, square the power, and shift to the next bit. All matrices have size two, so each multiplication takes constant time. Reduce every sum and product modulo `1_000_000_007`; use a 64-bit intermediate for products in C++.

### Edge cases

Lengths one and two both have answer two. A same-character string of even length is invalid, and different recursive concatenation trees for the same run sequence must not be counted as different strings. Counting run lengths avoids that duplicate counting.
4073.timeComplexity: O(log n) modular arithmetic operations using exponentiation of fixed-size 2×2 matrices.
4073.spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space for the fixed-size matrices and counters.
checks: Independently constructed sets of good strings using the original recursive concatenation rule for every length 1–12, then compared their sizes with the supplied matrix-exponentiation algorithm’s Python equivalent. All matched.
Counts for lengths 1–12 were 2, 2, 4, 6, 10, 16, 26, 42, 68, 110, 178, and 288. Python2 compatibility adjustments for this execution preserved integer division and reusable zip columns.

4077.title: Minimize Inversions in a Prefix Tree
4077.explanationMarkdown:
### Separate each pair at the node where its order is decided

Replace each word index with its position in `target`. An inversion then means that a larger target position appears before a smaller one.

In a preorder traversal, all marked words below one child form a contiguous block. Reordering that child's descendants changes inversions inside the block, but cannot change the number of inversions between that entire block and another child block. This lets us optimize each trie node independently.

Process trie nodes from leaves toward the root. The implementation can use reverse creation order because a child is always created after its parent. For each processed subtree, keep its marked words' target positions in sorted order. These lists are summaries for counting pairs; they are not the proposed traversal order.

### Compute the cost of putting one child before another

For child lists `A` and `B`, let `cost[A][B]` count pairs `x in A`, `y in B` with `x > y`. If the whole `A` block appears first, exactly these pairs become inversions. Since the lists are sorted, scan `A` while advancing a pointer through the elements of `B` smaller than the current `x`.

Target positions are unique, so every cross pair is an inversion in exactly one of the two possible block orders. Consequently `cost[B][A] = len(A) * len(B) - cost[A][B]`.

### Choose the child order with subset DP

A node has at most ten children. Let `dp[mask]` be the minimum cross-block inversion count after placing the children in `mask`. If child `c` is appended last, the new cost is the sum of `cost[a][c]` over children `a` already placed:

`dp[mask] = min_c(dp[mask without c] + sum_a cost[a][c])`.

The code precomputes these sums in `cost_total` by removing the lowest set bit, so each candidate transition uses an already available total. Add the optimal full-mask cost to the answer.

### Account for a word that is a prefix of other words

A marked node must be recorded before all its descendants; child ordering cannot change that. Its unavoidable inversions equal the number of descendant target positions smaller than its own. Merge the child lists, include the node's own target position if present, and use binary search to count smaller positions. The node's own equal position is not included in that count.

Every pair of distinct words is counted exactly once: either when one is the other's marked ancestor, or at their lowest common ancestor where they occupy different child blocks. The independent minimum child orders therefore combine into a globally optimal traversal.

### Complexity and edge cases

Let `L` be the total number of characters across the words, `T` the number of trie nodes, and `d_v` the number of children at node `v`. Pair counting and heap merging revisit each target position only along its word's prefix path. The alphabet bound of ten keeps each node's subset search small. Single-child nodes need no ordering DP. Prefix words still require their fixed inversion contribution, even if there is only one child.
4077.timeComplexity: O(L + n log n + Σ_v d_v·2^d_v) for the fixed 10-letter alphabet; the subset term is needed only at branching nodes and is bounded by O(n·10·2^10). Here n is the number of words, L is their total length, and d_v ≤ 10 is a node’s child count. With the alphabet treated as fixed this is O(L + n log n).
4077.spaceComplexity: O(10T + n + 10·2^10) for trie nodes, live sorted rank lists, and reusable subset-DP buffers, where T ≤ L + 1. This is O(L + n) for the fixed alphabet.
checks: Compared the supplied algorithm’s Python equivalent with independently enumerating all preorder traversals obtained from all child permutations. Tested all nonempty word subsets of {a,b,aa,ab,ba,bb} and all target permutations: 1,956 cases, all matched.
These cases cover marked ancestors, unary paths, several branching levels, reversed target orders, and a single word. The Python test harness supplied the heapq import used by the implementation.

4081.title: Prime Subset Selection II
4081.explanationMarkdown:
### Solve the three objectives in their required order

First maximize the sum, then minimize the number of selected primes, and only then minimize the sorted answer lexicographically. A suffix dynamic program records the information needed to handle all three without storing every possible subset.

Generate the increasing list of primes up to `n`. The supplied code uses a linear sieve: each composite is marked through its smallest prime factor, avoiding repeated work across different prime factors.

Let `dp[i][t]` be the minimum number of primes needed to make the exact sum `t` using only primes from index `i` onward. Impossible sums have value infinity. The base row has `dp[P][0] = 0` and every positive sum impossible, where `P` is the number of generated primes.

For prime `p = primes[i]`, either skip it or select it once:

`dp[i][t] = min(dp[i + 1][t], 1 + dp[i + 1][t - p])`.

Use the second option only when `t >= p` and the suffix sum is reachable. Both options advance to `i + 1`, which prevents selecting the same prime twice. Fill the rows in decreasing index order.

Scan sums from `s` down to zero. The first reachable sum is the largest possible sum; its value in `dp[0]` is the smallest number of primes among subsets with that sum.

### Reconstruct the lexicographically smallest optimum

Scan primes in increasing order while tracking the remaining target sum. Select the current prime whenever

`dp[i + 1][target - p] == dp[i][target] - 1`.

This equality says that choosing `p` still permits the required remaining sum using exactly the optimal number of primes. If it is feasible, any optimal solution that skips `p` must begin with a larger remaining prime, so including `p` is lexicographically better. If it is not feasible, every optimal completion must skip it. After selecting a prime, subtract it from the target and continue; the resulting array is already increasing.

### Why all priorities are preserved

The descending sum search fixes the primary objective before reconstruction. The DP value fixes the minimum cardinality for that sum. During reconstruction, each greedy choice is checked against the suffix DP, so it cannot sacrifice either objective. Choosing the smallest feasible next prime then gives the lexicographically smallest array among all remaining optimal completions.

The alternative `Solution2` in the source stores `(count, sorted list)` directly for each sum and compares these pairs. It visits primes in decreasing order and sums in decreasing order, so prepending the current prime keeps the list sorted and each prime is used at most once. This saves DP rows but pays for copying and comparing lists.

### Edge cases

If `n < 2` or `s < 2`, only sum zero is reachable and the result is empty. If the sum of every available prime fits, selecting all of them maximizes the sum. Distinct subsets with the same sum must still be compared first by cardinality; a lexicographically smaller but longer subset is not preferred.
4081.timeComplexity: Primary solution: O(n + P·s), where P is the number of primes ≤ n. The linear sieve costs O(n), the suffix DP O(P·s), and reconstruction O(P+s). Alternative Solution2: O(n + P·s·ℓ), where ℓ is the maximum length of a feasible prime subset, due to list copying and comparison.
4081.spaceComplexity: Primary solution: O(n + P·s), including the sieve and suffix DP. Alternative Solution2: O(n + s·ℓ), including its stored candidate lists.
checks: Compared the supplied primary algorithm’s Python equivalent against exhaustive enumeration of all distinct-prime subsets for every n from 1–25 and every s from 1–50: 1,250 cases, all matched.
The independent oracle orders candidate subsets by descending sum, ascending length, then lexicographic order, checking all three priorities and empty-subset cases.
